subject: paediatrics
title: Coarctation of the Aorta, Eisenmenger and Ebstein Anomaly

steps.tx: Juxtaductal aortic narrowing creates significant mechanical impedance to systemic arterial outflow. The obstructive lesion **coarctation of the aorta** involves focal stenosis of the aortic arch lumen, situated almost invariably directly opposite the insertion of the ductus arteriosus. Accounting for eight percent of congenital cardiac defects, it exhibits a strong association with bicuspid aortic valve in eighty percent of cases and Turner syndrome 45X.
steps.say: Coarctation of the aorta is a focal constriction opposite the ductus arteriosus. Associated with bicuspid aortic valves and Turner syndrome, it causes upper body hypertension.

vis.alt: Radiographic view of thoracic aorta showing coarctation figure-of-3 and rib notching.
vis.caption: Aortic coarctation demonstrating figure-of-3 sign on superior mediastinum and inferior rib notching. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Differential vascular perfusion between upper and lower extremities provides the clinical diagnostic hallmark. Palpation reveals marked **radio-femoral delay**, where the femoral arterial pulse is noticeably delayed and diminished compared to the synchronous radial pulse. Blood pressure measurement confirms upper extremity hypertension with lower extremity hypotension, demonstrating a systolic blood pressure gradient of twenty millimetres of mercury or greater between arm and leg.
steps.say: Radio-femoral delay and lower extremity hypotension confirm coarctation. A systolic blood pressure gradient of twenty millimetres or greater between arm and calf is diagnostic.

left.title: Upper Extremity Findings
points: Hypertensive systolic blood pressure in right arm
Strong, bounding radial and brachial pulses
Prominent carotid arterial pulsations in neck
Early risk of cerebral Berry aneurysm rupture

right.title: Lower Extremity Findings
points: Diminished, weak, or completely absent femoral pulses
Noticeable time lag behind simultaneous radial beat
Hypotension in lower limbs (systolic calf BP < arm BP)
Cold feet and exertional lower extremity claudication

steps.tx: Spontaneous postnatal ductal constriction precipitates sudden cardiogenic shock in neonates. In neonates with severe coarctation, systemic perfusion to the lower body relies upon ductal patency; when the ductus closes, the infant develops **neonatal duct-dependent shock**, presenting with sudden pallor, tachypnoea, metabolic lactic acidosis, and oliguria. Immediate resuscitation mandates continuous intravenous infusion of prostaglandin E1 to reopen the ductus and restore lower body perfusion.
steps.say: When the ductus closes, neonates with critical coarctation collapse in cardiogenic shock with absent femoral pulses. Continuous intravenous prostaglandin E1 reopens the ductus to restore perfusion.

rows: Severe left ventricular failure and hypertension

steps.tx: Chronic collateral blood flow through intercostal arteries erodes the cortical margins of ribs. In children older than five years, plain chest radiography demonstrates **inferior rib notching**, or Roesler's sign, appearing as scalloped erosions along the inferior margins of the third through eighth ribs caused by tortuous, dilated intercostal collaterals. The left superior mediastinal shadow shows the figure-of-3 sign, formed by pre-stenotic and post-stenotic aortic dilatations.
steps.say: Dilated intercostal collateral vessels erode the undersides of the ribs, producing rib notching on chest X-rays. The aortic shadow displays the classic figure-of-three sign.

left.title: Roesler Rib Notching Sign
points: Scalloped cortical indentations on lower rib borders
Involves 3rd to 8th ribs bilaterally
Snares 1st and 2nd ribs (supplied by costocervical trunk)
Evolves with age; rarely visible under 5 years

right.title: Figure-of-3 Aortic Sign
points: Upper curve: dilated left subclavian and aortic arch
Central indentation: narrow coarctation stenosis
Lower curve: post-stenotic dilatation of descending aorta
Barium swallow shows corresponding E-sign

steps.tx: Irreversible remodeling of the pulmonary arterial microvasculature reverses intracardiac shunt direction. Chronic uncorrected left-to-right shunting from large VSDs or PDAs induces medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis of pulmonary arterioles, culminating in **Eisenmenger syndrome physiology**. When pulmonary vascular resistance equals or exceeds systemic vascular resistance, the shunt reverses right-to-left, transforming an acyanotic patient into an irreversibly cyanotic state with digital clubbing.
steps.say: Eisenmenger syndrome occurs when high pulmonary blood flow causes irreversible vascular remodeling. Pulmonary resistance exceeds systemic pressure, reversing the shunt to right-to-left.

rows: Defect closure is curative and safe

steps.tx: Establishing Eisenmenger syndrome permanently contraindicates surgical or transcatheter defect closure. Attempting surgical closure in fixed pulmonary hypertension precipitates acute fatal right ventricular failure, as the right ventricle loses its pop-off decompression pathway across the defect. Medical management relies on pulmonary vasodilators like endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan) and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (sildenafil), alongside targeted venesection for **symptomatic hyperviscosity syndrome** (headaches, visual disturbances).
steps.say: Once Eisenmenger syndrome develops, surgical closure is strictly contraindicated because the right ventricle fails. Medical therapy uses sildenafil and bosentan to dilate pulmonary vessels.

left.title: Absolute Contraindication to Surgery
points: Fixed pulmonary vascular resistance >8 Wood units
Negative pulmonary vasoreactivity testing
Surgical closure leads to acute fatal RV failure
VSD acts as vital pop-off decompression valve

right.title: Advanced Medical Management
points: Oral endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan)
Oral PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil)
Prostacyclin analogues (treprostinil)
Targeted phlebotomy with isovolaemic replacement

steps.tx: Embryological failure of tricuspid delamination displaces the valve deep into the right ventricle. The congenital malformation **Ebstein anomaly of tricuspid valve** features downward apical displacement of the septal and posterior tricuspid leaflets into the right ventricular cavity, associated with first-trimester maternal lithium ingestion. This divides the right ventricle into an atrialized inlet portion and a small functional pumping chamber, precipitating tricuspid regurgitation.
steps.say: Ebstein anomaly features downward displacement of the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, linked to maternal lithium use. This creates an atrialized right ventricle and massive tricuspid leakage.

vis.alt: Chest radiograph showing box-shaped massive cardiomegaly in Ebstein anomaly.
vis.caption: Massive globular box-shaped cardiomegaly filling the thoracic cavity in neonatal Ebstein anomaly. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Extravagant tricuspid regurgitation and chamber enlargement produce a distinctive box-shaped cardiac contour. Chest radiography demonstrates **box-shaped cardiomegaly**, where the heart fills the entire thoracic cavity due to massive enlargement of the right atrium and atrialized right ventricle. Accessory atrioventricular pathways producing Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome occur in twenty-five percent of patients, triggering recurrent paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardias.
steps.say: Massive right atrial dilatation creates a huge box-shaped heart on chest X-rays. Accessory pathways cause Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and supraventricular tachycardia in a quarter of patients.

rows: Tall peaked P waves (Himalayan P waves)
Right heart failure and low cardiac output
Prolonged PR interval, right bundle branch block
Short PR interval with delta wave
